title: Halim
subtitle: Persian wheat and lamb porridge
excerpt: Halim is a thick, slow-cooked Persian porridge made from wheat, lamb, and spices, beaten together until the meat and grain merge into a dense, creamy mass. Topped with cinnamon, butter, and sugar, it is eaten as a warming breakfast or a restorative meal at any time of day.
sourceNotes: Halim is one of the oldest dishes in Persian and broader Middle Eastern cooking, eaten across Iran, Turkey (as 'keskek'), Pakistan, and India. The wheat-and-meat porridge is common to many cultures and appears under various names throughout the region.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well. Reheat gently with a splash of water, stirring to prevent sticking.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made the day it is served; can be reheated gently the next day.

content.text: Halim is ancient food. Whole wheat and lamb are cooked together for three hours until both have completely broken down and beaten into a single creamy mass. The result is a dish unlike most western cooking: deeply filling, almost velvety in texture, and powerfully savoury.

It is a breakfast dish in Iran, often bought from specialist stalls or made at home in winter. Eaten with a topping of cinnamon, butter, and a little sugar, the sweet-savoury balance is unexpected but works extremely well.
Whole wheat for halim is sold in Persian, Turkish, and South Asian grocers, sometimes labelled husked wheat or halim wheat. Soaking it overnight shortens the cooking time considerably.

items.prepNote: whole (husked) wheat berries soaked overnight; or bulgur wheat for a quicker version

content.text: Drain the soaked wheat. Place in a large saucepan with the lamb, onion, turmeric, cinnamon, salt, and half the butter. Cover with 2 litres of water. Bring to the boil, skim off any foam, then reduce to a low simmer. Cook covered for 2.5 to 3 hours until the wheat is completely soft and the lamb is very tender.
Remove the lamb and beat the mixture

Lift out the lamb pieces and the onion halves. Discard the onion. Use two forks to shred the lamb into small fibres. Return the shredded lamb to the pot. Beat the mixture vigorously with a heavy wooden spoon for 10 minutes, or use a hand mixer on low speed, until the wheat and lamb are completely combined into a thick, uniform porridge. Add the remaining butter and beat to incorporate.
Ladle into bowls. Drizzle with melted butter, dust with cinnamon, and scatter sugar over the top if using. Serve immediately.

rows.cause: Wheat not soaked overnight or very old stock
rows.fix: Continue simmering for another 30 to 60 minutes. Old wheat grains can take much longer.

rows.cause: Too much water used or lid left off
rows.fix: Continue cooking uncovered on a medium heat, stirring constantly, until thickened to a porridge consistency.

rows.cause: Heat too high after adding butter
rows.fix: Keep at the lowest simmer possible once you begin beating. Stir continuously and use a heavy-based pan.

content.text: Some versions use chicken instead of lamb for a lighter result. In Turkey, a version called keskek uses whole wheat or barley beaten with chicken and is served at weddings. A small amount of saffron steeped in hot water can be beaten into the halim at the end.
Halim can be reheated the next day. Add a splash of water and stir constantly over low heat to loosen; it will thicken as it cools and needs liquid to return to a pourable consistency.

Halim is sold from street stalls and shops in Iran in the early morning, particularly on winter days and during Ramadan. It is also a home-cooked dish eaten after fasting or as a slow Sunday breakfast. The combination of wheat and meat cooked to a porridge appears in food history across Persia, Turkey, the Caucasus, South Asia, and the Arab world.
